steps: Unpack & check contents

Inspect for transit damage. The firebox holds the manual, two boxes of soapstone lining, 2 leveling bolts, 2 soapstone spacers, a metal installation label and 3 liner brackets; remove the packaging in the flue collar and above the baffle before installing the chimney.
Inspect the fireplace & chimney

Masonry fireplace and chimney must meet local code and be free of cracks, loose mortar, creosote, blockage or deterioration; clean or upgrade first. Check clearance to exposed and concealed combustibles; mesh caps need provision for regular cleaning, or remove the mesh.

Masonry or steel, including the damper plate, may be removed from the smoke shelf and adjacent damper frame to fit the liner, provided that does not weaken the structure or reduce protection for combustibles below code. Do not remove bricks or mortar from the existing fireplace (p. 5).

Not for installation in a bedroom. Not approved for a positive flue connection to the clay tile. Do not connect to a chimney flue serving another appliance or to air distribution ductwork (p. 5).
Lock open or remove the damper

Lock the throat damper open for liner access, or remove it. If removed, secure the metal plate (27009) from the owner's manual kit inside the masonry hearth, visible and easy to locate, to show the hearth was modified.
Hearth & floor protection

Noncombustible protection under and in front: 16" (USA) / 18" (Canada) without R-value on a hearth raised more than 5"; R 1.00 or more and 23" on a hearth lower than 5". Add D = B - (A - C) in front of the hearth extension when positive.
Check opening & clearances

Minimum masonry opening J 23 5/16", K 28 7/8", L 19 5/8" (Fig. 9); add 4" to the width for a fresh air intake. Combustible mantel shelf no deeper than 12" and at least 27" above the insert; other clearances per Fig. 9.
Prepare the insert

Empty the firebox and remove the front casting (two screws below the ash lip, tilt up and lift off the hanger tabs). With two or more people, lift it off the pallet and thread the leveling bolts into the 2 welded nuts at the lower rear corners; attach optional steel-surround brackets now.
Install the chimney liner

Continuous 6" listed stainless steel liner for solid fuel, from the insert to the top of the chimney (UL 1777, ULC S635 or CAN/ULC S640). A sheet-metal block-off plate is recommended, and at least 12" of rigid liner between the masonry top and the rain cap is strongly recommended.

Block-off plate: cut the pipe hole slightly larger than the liner and pass the liner through; secure the plate with masonry nails; seal plate-to-chimney joints with high temperature silicone and pipe-to-plate with stove cement. In Canada, CSA B365 permits Roxul-type wool stuffed around the liner at the throat instead, though it is less efficient.

Chimney height: at least 3 ft (1 m) above the highest point of contact with the roof, and 2 ft (60 cm) higher than any roof line or obstacle within 10 ft (3 m) (p. 21).
Set the insert & connect the liner

Slide the insert in until the top lip of the air jacket is flush with the fireplace facing, and connect the liner to the flue collar on top. Use the 3 supplied brackets with a liner starter adapter, the Liner Hook-Up Starter Collar (94-67500), or as a last resort the offset adapter (5700-007).

Option 1: fit the starter adapter supplied with the liner per its maker's instructions. Fasten the three brackets on top of the insert with the three supplied screws, long end to the insert; insert the liner into the flue collar and secure it to the brackets with three self-tapping screws (not included).

Option 2: the Liner Hook-Up Starter Collar #94-67500 (HearthStone's recommendation), per its own instructions.

Option 3: liner offset adapter #5700-007, only if no other option is possible and the fireplace plus chimney is at least 20 feet tall. It restricts exhaust flow and may cause smoke roll-out when the door is opened to reload. Fit the three brackets as in option 1, then follow the kit's manual.

If lag bolts or anchors will secure the insert, mark the holes with the unit in place, then remove it and set the anchors.
Level, trim & front casting

Level with the rear bolts and fit any optional steel surround, lower panel or surround extension (surround set 4" back, or 2" with cut panels). Move the blower switch plate to the front casting's lower rear left corner without disconnecting its wires, then rehang the casting and refit its two screws.

Rehanging the casting: pass the air control handle through the opening below the ash lip and don't pinch the blower switch wires. Lift the casting onto the tabs on top of the insert, let it rest on the top edge of the firebox, and slide it left or right to center it on the door; the door must open fully without touching it. The two screws pass through the square holes in the hanger brackets.

Blower: 115V-60Hz-30W tangential blower, 90 CFM, 96" 18-3 SJT power cord, F110-20F thermodisc (parts list, p. 36). Keep the cord off every insert surface and never run it beneath the insert (p. 23).
Line the firebox & final check

Fit the soapstone: floor stones first, then the 2 spacer channels along the sides, then side and rear stones with their tops behind the retaining steel. Confirm the door opens fully and seals shut, the air control moves left and right, and the blower turns on and off.

9" x 4.5" x 1.25"14
9" x 4.25" x 1.25"2
9" x 2" x 1.25"4
6.5" x 4.5" x 1.25"2
Spacer channel2

Stone positions are on the lining diagram (p. 17). To replace stones later: let the insert and ashes cool fully, clean out the ash, remove the rear stones, then the sides, then the floor; reinstall in reverse with the top edges behind the retaining steel (p. 32).

panels.title: Insert smokes
items: Operating technique → open the air fully one minute before opening the door
Cold chimney or reverse draft → preheat the chimney; briefly open a window in the room
Blocked chimney → check chimney and stovepipe for blockage or creosote
Oversized / undersized / too-short chimney → reline; draft inducer or replace; lengthen
Air leaking into the chimney → seal connections and openings; check clean-out doors
Improper fuel, or another appliance on the flue → seasoned dry cordwood; disconnect others and seal

panels.title: Back-puffing or gas explosions
items: Operating technique → air fully open one minute before opening the door and for a few minutes after reloading
Extra-low burn rate → burn at a higher rate
Chimney down-draft → install a chimney cap
Excessive ash build-up → empty ashes more often; avoid poor-quality or green wood

panels.title: Uncontrolled or short burn
items: Unsealed or open door, or leaking glass gasket → close tightly; replace gaskets
Excessive draft → check the install, run on low; stovepipe damper(s) for draft over 0.1 WC
Extra-long or oversized chimney → shorten or add damper(s); reline to the proper diameter
High winds or hilltop location → install a chimney cap

panels.title: Insufficient heat
items: Poor, low-Btu or green wood → air-dried wood, at least one year; high-Btu species
Low burn rate → operate at a higher burn rate
Cold exterior chimney → reline or insulate
Leaky stovepipe or chimney → check install; insulated prefab or properly sized masonry chimney
Heat loss from the house → insulation, efficient windows, caulk and seal openings
Excessive ash build-up → empty ashes more often

fire.title: Building a fire
fire.html:
Burn the fire right on the firebox floor. Don't use a log grate or anything else to raise it.

  1. Open the door. Put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox.
  2. Build a tee-pee of about 10 pieces of kindling over the paper, each about 1/2" thick and 10" to 16" long.
  3. Open the air control fully: move the lever under the ash lip all the way left.
  4. Light the paper. Leave the door slightly open for a moment, until the kindling catches and the chimney starts to draw.
  5. Close the door and let the fire burn. Keep the door closed while the insert is in use.
  6. Once the kindling is burning, add logs, small ones first. Keep them toward the center, away from the glass.
  7. Set the burn rate with the lever: left for more heat, right for less.

Reloading

  • Open the air fully one minute before you open the door. Then open the door just a crack, pause, and open it all the way, so smoke clears first.
  • Load onto a bed of hot, red coals. Leave a small valley in the coals behind the lower primary air opening so the new wood relights faster.
  • After reloading, burn with the air fully open for 15 to 20 minutes.
Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen up a fire.

breakin.title: Breaking in your insert
breakin.html:
Your soapstone has to be seasoned. Its natural moisture must be driven out slowly, and the furnace cement must cure. Over-firing a new insert may crack the soapstone or damage other parts.

Your first fire, and the first fire each season

  1. Twist five or six double sheets of newspaper in the center of the firebox. Crisscross about ten pieces of kindling over them, about 1/2" thick and 10" to 16" long.
  2. Open the air control fully (lever all the way left) and light the paper. Leave the door slightly open until the kindling catches, then close it.
  3. Keep a watchful eye. Hold a steady, low-heat fire: warm, not hot, to the touch. At most, add a few small chunks of wood.
  4. Once it's warm but not hot, close the air control (lever all the way right) and let the fire die out completely.
  5. Let the insert return to room temperature.
Too hot: visible steam, boiling moisture or hissing means the soapstone is too hot.

Smoke and smells at first are normal

Paints and oils give off some smoke and fumes during the first fires. Open a few windows if needed; it usually fades after 10 to 20 minutes. Early-season odors can also come from nearby dust, pet hair, solvents or new carpet. If an odor persists, call your dealer.

These cool fires can build creosote (flammable tar deposits) in the chimney fast and dirty the glass. Have the stovepipe and chimney checked once break-in is done.

air.title: Air control, burn rates & over-firing
air.html:
One lever under the ash lip controls the air. More air gives a faster fire and more heat; less air gives a slower fire and less heat. The lever never shuts the air off completely.

LowLever all the way right
Medium-lowFrom low, move it left a little less than 1/2"
Medium-highFrom low, move it left a little less than 1"
HighLever all the way left; load fully onto hot coals

Medium-low is the typical setting, and the best one if you'll leave the insert unattended. Long stretches on low can build creosote (flammable tar deposits in the chimney), so run on high once or twice a day for 35 to 45 minutes. The lowest setting is fixed at the factory, and altering it is against federal regulations.

Signs of over-firing

Over-firing means running hotter than a normal high burn. Watch for warped parts, short burn times, a roaring sound in the insert or chimney, or a discolored finish. Causes include too much draft, the wrong fuel, worn gaskets, or burning with the door open (fully open is allowed only with the fire screen in place). If you suspect over-firing, stop using the insert and call your dealer immediately.

Never over-fire your insert. It will damage the insert. Over-firing damage isn't covered. The manual says any signs of over-firing void your warranty.

wood.title: Choosing firewood
wood.html:
Burn only natural cordwood that is dry and seasoned. Air-dried hardwoods give higher efficiency and lower emissions than softwoods or green wood. Softwoods burn hotter and faster; hardwoods burn longer and make better coals. Logs can be up to 20" long.

Seasoning

  • Split, stack and air-dry green wood for one year. Green wood may give less than 2000 Btu per pound; dry wood up to 7000.
  • Seasoned wood is typically at or near 20% moisture. A hand-held moisture meter can check it.
  • Stack it on skids or blocks and cover only the top. Tarps over the sides trap moisture.

The manual's heat-value table rates hickory, white oak, black locust and apple high; sugar maple, red oak, white ash and yellow birch medium-high; aspen, balsam fir, white pine and white cedar low.

Never burn

Garbage or trash, lawn clippings, coal, charcoal, pellets, artificial or wax logs, compressed wood, kiln-dried, painted, treated (including pressure-treated) or unseasoned wood, plywood, particleboard, cardboard, paper products (including colored or glossy paper), driftwood (including salt-water driftwood) or other materials previously saturated with salt water, materials containing rubber (including tires), materials containing plastic, waste petroleum products, paints or paint thinners, solvents, asphalt products, materials containing asbestos, construction or demolition debris, railroad ties, manure or animal remains, highly volatile fuels or combustibles, or flammable fluids. Burning these materials may release toxic fumes, or make the insert ineffective and cause smoke. Using an unauthorized fuel such as coal could produce high levels of carbon dioxide in the living space, which at high levels could cause injury or death. Fire starters made of paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine for lighting.

Don't store firewood within the insert's clearances to combustibles, and never load ice-covered wood into a burning insert.

ash.title: Removing and disposing of ashes
ash.html:
Empty the ashes at the end of every week, sooner if the firebox is full. You can leave a thin layer in the firebox if you like.

  1. Let the fire die down or go out completely.
  2. Use a fireplace shovel. Push large live coals to the side and take out only the finer ash.
  3. Don't let ash build up around the door opening. It can spill out, or pack into the gasket channel and stop the door sealing.

Disposal

  • Put the ashes straight into a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Nothing else goes in it, and don't pour water in.
  • Close the lid. Set the container on a noncombustible floor or on the ground outside, well away from anything that burns, liquid fuels and vehicles. Never put it on a combustible surface or vinyl flooring, because it could be hot.
  • Keep the ashes in the closed container until all the coals have thoroughly cooled, including before you bury or spread them.
Never put ashes in wooden or plastic containers, in trash cans with other trash, or in paper or plastic bags, no matter how long the fire has been out. Coals in ash can stay hot for several days.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
The door glass is a tough, clear ceramic made for temperatures up to 2300° F. Clean it only when the fire is out and the glass is cool.

  1. Dip a damp paper towel in white ash and rub the inside of the glass in a circular motion.
  2. When the deposits are off, finish with a commercial stove-glass cleaner from your dealer, inside and out, following its directions.
  3. Wipe the cleaner off with a soft cloth or black-and-white newsprint.
No razor blades, steel wool or abrasives. Scratches weaken the glass. Use only a cleaner made for woodstoves.

Glass that always stays dirty means your fires run too cool or your wood is wet, which also raises the risk of creosote.

Cracked or chipped glass

Don't run the insert with broken glass, and don't strike or slam the door. Replace the glass right away with the ceramic glass made for this insert, from your dealer (glass kit 94-58505: glass and gasket).

The glass replacement procedure on p. 30 prints the required glass kit as 96-58405; the replacement kit list on p. 37 gives 94-58505, glass kit: glass and gasket.
Note: p. 30 warns that only a qualified service person should replace the glass panel; the same page also says to wear work gloves and safety glasses "if you replace the glass yourself."

chimney.title: Chimney, creosote & door seal
chimney.html:
Slow, cool fires give off tar and vapors that condense in the chimney as creosote. If it ignites, it burns extremely hot and can damage the chimney or even destroy the house.

Check and clean

  • Check daily for creosote buildup until experience shows how often you need to clean to be safe.
  • Inspect the chimney connector and chimney at least every two months in the heating season, and at least monthly once buildup starts. Check the top of the chimney, where it's coolest, as well as near the insert.
  • Remove creosote once it's more than 1/4" thick. A certified chimney sweep should do it; your dealer can name one.
  • Before each heating season, have the whole system professionally inspected, cleaned and repaired if needed.

Prevent it

Burn with the air fully open for 35 to 45 minutes every day, and for 15 to 20 minutes after each reload.

Door seal and season's end

Every other month, with the insert cool, close the door on a dollar bill. If it pulls out with no resistance, adjust the latch or replace the gasket. Replace the door gasket every two to three seasons, or when it's worn or loose, with HearthStone replacement gaskets.

At season's end, take apart and clean the chimney connector, replacing rusted or deteriorated pieces, and inspect the chimney. The checklist also says to clean out the inside of the insert thoroughly.

blower.title: Using the blower
blower.html:
The blower comes installed, under the insert behind the front casting. It moves more air through the heat exchanger and circulates warm air into the room.

Position 3 · automaticA heat sensor starts it when the insert is hot enough and stops it once the insert cools
Position 1 · manualRuns any time
Position 2Stops the blower

Let the insert reach operating temperature, about one hour, before turning the blower on. Extra air too early pulls heat away and affects start-up combustion efficiency.

Used regularly, the blower adds a small efficiency gain, up to 2%. It won't make up for an insert that's too small for the space.

Keep the cord clear. Don't let the blower cord touch any surface of the insert, and don't run it under the insert. That risks electrical shock or fire damage.

safety.title: Safety & chimney fires
safety.html:
• The insert is hot while it's running. Keep children, pets, clothing and furniture away, since touching it can burn. Use fireplace gloves.
  • Keep furniture, drapes and other combustibles at least 36" from the insert. Never put clothing or candles on it.
  • Keep the door closed while burning. With the optional fire screen the door may be fully open, but never leave the insert unattended that way.
  • Install smoke and carbon monoxide (CO) detectors throughout the heated space, including bedrooms and hallways, and test them. Keep an "A B C" fire extinguisher handy.
  • Never slam the door or use it to force wood in.

If you have a chimney fire

  1. If the fire is too threatening, leave and call the fire department right away. If not:
  2. Close the air control.
  3. Close the stovepipe damper, if you have one.
  4. Keep the front door closed.
Never throw water on the insert, stovepipe or chimney. The heat turns it to steam instantly and can cause serious injury.

Afterward, leave the air closed and let the fire die out completely. Have the insert and chimney checked by a certified sweep or fire marshal, and fix any damage before using it again.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
HearthStone's limited warranty covers defects in material or workmanship for the original retail purchaser only, on an insert installed by an authorized HearthStone dealer or their designated representative. It isn't transferable and starts on the date of the original invoice. "Limited Lifetime" means 10 years.

Limited LifetimeExternal stone; cast iron not listed elsewhere
5 yearsDoor handles and latches; steel components and firebox
2 yearsAppliance electrical and gas components; refractory stone, vermiculite panels, baffles
1 yearEnamel finish against peeling or fading; accessories; glass; all components not listed elsewhere

Labor is paid in the first year only if a dealer installed the insert. Parts shipping is paid for the first 90 days.

Not covered

  • Over-firing, or not following the manual or building codes
  • Work by anyone other than an authorized HearthStone dealer
  • Expansion noise, odors, scratches, and hairline stone cracks that don't affect operation
Note: the warranty grid on p. 41 covers refractory stone and baffles for 2 years and glass for 1 year, but exclusion 3 on p. 42 excludes repair or replacement of wear parts (parts subject to normal wear and tear, such as gaskets, baffles, refractory materials and glass).

Claims go through your dealer. Registering online is recommended, but sending in the registration isn't a condition of coverage.

specOutput.title: Heat output
specOutput.html:
Maximum heat output44,500 BTUs per hour (cordwood)
Heated areaup to a maximum of 2,000 sq ft
Burn timeHeatLife up to 8+ hrs
Tested output range (p. 2)14,200 to 44,500 Btu
Maker's website: BTU: Up to 70,000.
Maker's website: HeatLife: 10 Hours of heat.

Based on independent laboratory test results. Insulation, windows, floor plan, fireplace placement and fuel quality can reduce the area heated. Wood per cubic foot of firebox varies from 10 to 25 lbs with species, moisture and packing.

The manual says not to treat the insert as the sole heat source and strongly recommends a conventional backup heating system.

specEmissions.title: EPA rating & efficiency
specEmissions.html:
Particulate emissions2.3 g/hr
Weighted average efficiency72% (HHV)
Average CO, all burn categories69 g/hr
Maker's website: EPA Certified: 1.54 g/hr.
Maker's website: Efficiency: 69% HHV.

Certified to the U.S. EPA 2020 particulate emissions standard using cord wood (CFR 40 part 60, subpart AAA; ASTM E3053-17; ALT-125). Efficiency is weighted across the 4 burn rate categories (CSA B415.1-10 methodology). Test logs were 16 ± 1 inches long, hard maple. The rating paragraph on p. 2 prints the rate as "2.3 gr/hr"; the specifications on p. 7 give 2.3 g/hr.

Loading by burn rate (p. 8)

High: air fully open. Crisscross eight 2" x 2" pieces, then 10 to 16 kindling pieces in three layers, with five knotted sheets of paper on top. Light it with the door ajar at 90° until the kindling and the first row of small pieces are burning, then close the door. When only faint flames remain at the back, break up the ashes, level the coal bed and load five logs: 3 tight together, one inch from the rear firebrick, 2 on top east-west. Door ajar one inch for 1 minute maximum, then close.

Medium / low: on a two-inch red coal bed, three logs east-west with air space around them, two on top angled 20°. Door ajar at 90° about 5 min, then close it with the air open; after about 10 more minutes close the air completely (low) or halfway (medium), gradually.

The manufacturer-set minimum low burn rate must not be altered.

specFirebox.title: Firebox
specFirebox.html:
Overall firebox volume2.4 cubic feet
EPA loading volume1.95 cubic feet
Maximum log lengthup to 20" (50.8 cm)

Soapstone-lined firebox with four secondary air tubes and a C-cast baffle (20" x 12 1/2" x 1 1/4"). Burn directly on the firebox floor; no grate. Secondary air tubes can be replaced without removing the baffle board (p. 33).

specFlue.title: Flue, liner & chimney
specFlue.html:
Connector6" (152 mm) diameter
Metal chimney6" (152 mm) inside diameter
Masonry chimney6" (152 mm) round flue · 8" x 8" (203 x 203 mm) square flue

Connect only to a listed stainless steel liner for solid fuel: continuous, 6" diameter, from the insert to the top of the chimney, meeting CAN/ULC-S635 Class 3 or CAN/ULC-S640 (p. 5); liners listed UL 1777, ULC S635 or CAN/ULC S640 (p. 18). Install only within a lined masonry chimney and masonry fireplace built for solid fuel. No positive flue connection to the clay tile, no flue shared with another appliance, no air distribution ductwork.

A chimney of at least 5 inches is permitted in Canada only, if verified and authorized by a qualified installer; reduce the liner below 6" only if the masonry chimney is taller than 20 feet (p. 18). A minimum 12" of rigid liner between the top of the masonry chimney and the rain cap is strongly recommended.

Height: at least 3 ft (1 m) above the highest point of contact with the roof, and 2 ft (60 cm) higher than any roof line or obstacle within 10 ft (3 m) (p. 21).

specOpening.title: Minimum masonry opening & combustion air
specOpening.html:
J23 5/16" (592 mm)
K28 7/8" (733 mm)
L19 5/8" (498 mm) without surround extension · 17 5/8" or 15 5/8" with it

The manual keys these letters to its clearance figure (Figure 9, p. 14); read J and L off the drawing. The footnote on K says to add a minimum of 4" to the width of the opening where a fresh air intake is needed (5"Ø fresh air intake kit AC01298, p. 36).

Combustion air (p. 22)

Room air is the safest, most reliable supply. Outside air may be needed if the insert won't draw steadily or back-drafts, other fuel-fired equipment smells or rolls out smoke, opening a window slightly on a calm day helps, the house is tightly sealed or has exhaust devices, windows show heavy winter condensation, or a ventilation system is installed (p. 6). A wall intake can pull exhaust backwards in wind: if smoke puffs in windy weather, disconnect the duct to test, and check it for soot at each yearly cleaning. In Canada outside air isn't required, but a CO detector is required in the room where the insert is installed.

specFloor.title: Hearth & floor protection
specFloor.html:
Protect combustible flooring with noncombustible material under the insert and extending in front of it. The hearth extension's depth counts toward the floor protector.

Hearth raised more than 5" (127 mm)no R-value; 16" (406 mm) USA · 18" (457 mm) Canada in front
Hearth lower than 5" (127 mm)R-value of 1.00 or more; 23" (584 mm) in front

Extra protection: D = B - (A - C), where A is the hearth extension, B the required protection and C the air-jacket projection (0" standard, 2" or 4" with the surround extension). If D is zero or negative, none is needed; if positive, add at least D in front of the hearth extension.

R-values add: four inches of brick (R 0.8) plus 1 inch of Durock® (R 0.52) gives 1.32, which meets 1.00. With known k values, R = thickness / k (p. 13). Side extensions (M, N) appear only as lettered dimensions in Figure 5. Some LVP and LVT flooring begins to warp at 110° Fahrenheit; extra shielding may be needed (p. 12).

Note: for a hearth exactly 5" high, the pages differ: p. 11 calls for the R-value protector only when the hearth is lower than 5" (a hearth at least 5" high takes 16"/18" without R-value), while p. 12 applies R 1.00 and 23" to a hearth 5" or less and p. 13 drops the R-value only above 5".

conflicts.issue: Glass kit part number: 96-58405 in the glass replacement procedure vs 94-58505 (glass kit: glass and gasket) in the replacement kit list.

review.notes: Single installation & operation manual (R 6/5/23); printed footer page numbers match physical pages. Not transcribed because the text never defines the letters: clearances H, Q and maximum thicknesses O, P on Fig. 9 (p. 14) (F 16" and G 9" are listed by letter in specClear, next to the website's side-trim and side-wall clearances), floor-protection side dimensions M/N on Fig. 5 (p. 11) and the figure values next to 'E' on p. 12; drawers point to the figures. Minimum masonry opening J/K/L is given with the manual's letters; only K is tied to the width (fresh-air footnote). Warranty grid (p. 41): only rows marked in both the Wood and Gas columns are listed, grouped under the period labels as laid out (labels sit on the first row of each group); single-mark rows (clean burning air supply system*, burner and logs, ash grate) can't be assigned to a column from the text and were left out, and the asterisk has no footnote in the text. Emission rate printed '2.3 gr/hr' (p. 2) vs '2.3 g/hr' (p. 7); guide uses g/hr. Kindling 10" to 16" is converted as 254 to 457 mm (break-in fire) and 254 to 406 mm (everyday fire), both p. 26; guide uses inches only. Troubleshooting chart (p. 39) says 'empty the ash pan' although the manual describes shoveling ash out of the firebox (p. 27); guide says 'empty ashes'. Cross-reference errors in the manual: p. 9 sends Minimum Masonry Opening to page 13 (it is p. 14); p. 5 cites 'page 124' for the 36" rule; p. 23 and p. 27 cite Figure 24 for the controls/air lever (Figure 24 is the fire-screen 'Open Door' figure on p. 28). Periodic checklist (p. 6) is two-column: 'clean out the inside of the insert' and 'inspect all door gasket material' sit at the top of the right column, most likely the end of the season list; the chimney drawer words them without an interval. p. 8 prints separate loading instructions for high and medium/low burn rates; summarized in the EPA drawer. The 'CO detector is required in the room' sentence (p. 22) sits in the Canada combustion-air paragraph; p. 2 'highly recommends' smoke and CO detectors throughout. Blower electrical data (115V-60hZ-30W, 90 CFM, 96" 18-3 SJT cord) comes from the parts list (p. 36), written 60Hz in the guide. The manual never says non-catalytic; it describes secondary air tubes and a baffle. No error-code table, so codes is empty. Oct 12 edit: the catalog's minimum fireplace opening (29 in. W x 24 in. H x 16 in. D) is in the catalog features only; website.json has no such row and the product page (checked Oct 12) prints no opening size, so specOpening carries no website note for it. Website rows 'Non-catalytic' and 'Finish' skipped: the manual doesn't cover them.
